1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4.background: Named after Szymon Winawer and pioneered by Aron Nimzowitsch and Mikhail Botvinnik. Thanks in great part to Botvinnik in the 1940s it became the most often seen reply to 3.Nc3, until 3...Nf6 revived in the 1980s and overtook it in popularity.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5.strategy: Pushes past the pin: with the c3 knight tied down, e4 cannot be defended by a recapture, so the pawn advances and gains space, supported by d4. The centre closes, White has more room on the kingside, and Black attacks the base of the chain.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Advance Variation

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Ne2.strategy: A gambit: the knight develops and leaves e4 to be taken. If Black accepts, a quick a3 puts the question to the bishop, and when it takes on c3 the knight recaptures, so White keeps a healthy pawn structure and a lead in development, but must show compensation for the pawn.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Ne2.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Alekhine-Maróczy Gambit

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.exd5.strategy: Resolves the tension by trading pawns, which frees Black's c8 bishop. With Nc3 and ...Bb4 added to the exchange structure, White can provoke ...Bxc3 with a3 and get an asymmetrical pawn structure, so the game is less drawish than the plain exchange.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.exd5.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Delayed Exchange Variation

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd3.strategy: Defends e4 with a developing move, the natural reflex, and keeps the tension. But it blocks the queen's support of d4 and creates no real problems: Black can take on e4 or strike at d4 and reach equality without difficulty.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3.strategy: Asks the bishop to decide at once. After ...Bxc3+ bxc3 White has the bishop pair and a half-open b-file, and Black's kingside lacks its dark-squared bishop, but the doubled pawns are a lasting liability and e4 needs looking after.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd2.strategy: Breaks the pin with a developing move but does not defend e4, so Black can simply take the pawn. White must find compensation in quick piece play against g7, which has no bishop at f8 to guard it; if that comes to nothing, White is just a pawn down.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd2.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Fingerslip Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd2.background: Frank Marshall first played it, against Mikhail Chigorin in 1901; Rashid Nezhmetdinov also played it, notably against Mikhail Tal. The name is said to come from a game between Alexander Alekhine and Salomon Flohr, in which Alekhine wanted to play the Bogoljubow Variation but mixed up his move order and played 4.Bd2 instead of 4.e5 c5 5.Bd2.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3 Bxc3+.strategy: Takes the knight before it can be chased, doubling White's pawns on the c-file at the cost of the dark-squared bishop. That bishop is Black's good piece and its absence leaves the dark squares near the king, g7 above all, short of cover, but the damaged pawn structure is a lasting trump.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd2 dxe4.strategy: Accepts the gambit: White broke the pin without defending e4, so Black wins a pawn and opens the centre. White now has to prove that quick development and play against g7 are worth the pawn.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd2 Ne7.strategy: Declines the pawn and develops, supporting the d5 pawn and keeping the structure intact. It is safe, but it hands White time to untangle, where taking the pawn makes White prove the compensation.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd3 c5.strategy: Strikes at the base of the white centre at once: with the bishop on d3 blocking the queen, d4 is attacked and has no defender, while the knight on c3 is pinned. White has to deal with the pawn before anything else.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Advance Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5.strategy: Attacks the base of White's pawn chain at once. With the knight already on c3, White cannot support d4 with a pawn, and the push also shuts the bishop's way home along the diagonal, so the bishop's future is in question straight away.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 Ne7.strategy: Develops the knight to the square it wants in the main line, where it supports the strike at d4 and can later reach g6 or f5, and keeps ...c5 in reserve. It mostly transposes, but White gets to pick a fifth move before the c-pawn has committed.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 Qd7.strategy: Steps the queen aside so that White's natural attack on g7 can be answered by driving the queen back with a pawn. The queen also blocks the c8 bishop and the knight's development, and White keeps the space advantage and the better chances.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 Qd7.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Petrosian Variation

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.exd5 exd5.strategy: Recaptures with the e-pawn, keeping a solid, symmetrical centre and the pin on c3. With the knight on c3 and the bishop on b4 inserted, the game is less drawish than the plain Exchange: White can try to show that the bishop is misplaced, usually by provoking the exchange on c3 with a3.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Ne2 dxe4.strategy: Accepts the gambit: the pawn on e4 is attacked by the d-pawn and cannot be defended by the pinned knight on c3, so Black wins it. White must now show that its lead in development is worth the pawn, and Black has to meet that with care.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Ne2 Nf6.strategy: Declines the offered pawn and develops, adding a second attacker on e4, which the pinned knight on c3 cannot defend. It sidesteps the gambit but passes up the extra pawn, and White can use the move to develop with threats, for instance by pinning the new knight.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3 Bxc3+ 5.b.strategy: The natural recapture: it gives White doubled c-pawns, but also a strong centre, a half-open b-file and the bishop pair against a kingside without its dark-squared bishop. White has attacking chances if the position stays open; in a closed game the pawn structure favours Black.
Takes the pawn that the last move left without a defender and opens the centre. Black is a pawn up for the moment, but must watch the dark squares around g7, where White's queen can strike.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3 Bxc3+ 5.b.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Winckelmann-Reimer Gambit
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3 Bxc3+ 5.b.strategy: Attacks the e4 pawn from the side and offers a second pawn as a gambit: if Black takes, White recaptures with a lead in development. Black does better to strike back in the centre at once.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd2 dxe4 5.Q.strategy: The point of the gambit: the queen attacks g7, which has lost its bishop's protection, and the e4 pawn at once. Black cannot keep everything, but White's queen comes out early and has to justify the pawn with threats.
Attacks the queen and defends e4 in one move, so Black keeps the extra pawn for now. The price is g7: if the queen takes it, Black gets time to harass the queen and the material stays level.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd2 dxe4 5.Q.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Fingerslip Variation, Kunin Double Gambit
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd2 dxe4 5.Q.background: Most opening databases call it the Kunin double gambit. The earliest game found with a player named Kunin is Vladimir Kunin against Oschengoit, 1958, which became a popular miniature. The line was known before: it had already appeared at the 1950 Candidates in a game between Isaac Boleslavsky and David Bronstein.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd2 dxe4 5.Q.strategy: Grabs a second pawn with the queen, but the queen is exposed in the centre while Black is undeveloped. Castling queenside lines the rook up behind the d2 bishop, so any bishop move uncovers an attack on the queen.

Takes the pawn and attacks the h8 rook in the same move. The queen is far from the rest of White's pieces, though, and Black's reply gains time to harass it, so White has to watch Black's lead in development.
Saves the rook with tempo by attacking the queen, and the rook takes the open g-file, pointing at g2. Black has traded the g7 pawn for activity and development.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd2 Ne7 5.Nb.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Fingerslip Variation, Schwarz's Line
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd2 Ne7 5.Nb.strategy: A sharp idea: the knight steps back so that the d2 bishop attacks the undefended bishop on b4 and asks for a trade. It costs two knight moves and leaves e4 hanging, so Black can take the pawn after the exchange while White is behind in development.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd3 c5 5.exd.strategy: Opens the centre by trading pawns instead of defending d4. The c3 knight is pinned, so it cannot retake on d5, and White relies on getting the pin undone with tempo; meanwhile d4 stays under fire.
Recaptures with the queen in the centre, where it hits both d4 and g2, and the pinned knight cannot challenge it. Black gets an active queen early, which White must try to hunt by unpinning.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd3 c5 5.exd.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Kondratiyev Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bd3 c5 5.exd.strategy: Breaks the pin by putting the bishop behind the knight, so that the knight now attacks the queen on d5. White offers the loose d4 and g2 pawns for tempo and development: a risky exchange of pawns for activity.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.a3.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Advance Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.a3.strategy: Chases the bishop, which has no retreat along its diagonal now that c5 is blocked: Black must trade it for the knight or pull it back offside. White gets the bishop pair and a strong centre at the price of doubled pawns, while the weakened dark squares near Black's king become targets.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.Bd2.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Bogoljubow Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.Bd2.strategy: Keeps the pawn structure intact: the bishop protects the knight, so a trade on c3 would no longer double White's pawns. It costs a tempo and does not chase the bishop, but it makes room for the knight to jump to b5, eyeing d6 and guarding d4.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.Qg4.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Advance Variation, Moscow Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.Qg4.strategy: Goes after g7 at once instead of preparing it: Black has no bishop on f8 to cover the pawn and will often let it go in exchange for the breakup of White's centre. A sharp, double-edged race between the queen sortie and Black's pressure on d4.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.a3 B.strategy: Takes the knight before it can be chased, doubling White's pawns for the dark-squared bishop. This is the main line: Black accepts a weakened kingside, which White's bishop pair and kingside space can attack, in exchange for the damage to White's structure and play against the d4 pawn.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.a3 B.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Retreat Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.a3 B.background: Sometimes called the Armenian Variation, because players from Armenia, most notably Rafael Vaganian, enriched its theory and practice.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.a3 B.strategy: Keeps the knight pinned and the bishop alive instead of trading it, which preserves Black's dark squares near the king. The bishop is offside on a5, though, and White can attack it at once, so Black must be ready for sharp tactics.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.a3 c.strategy: Takes the d4 pawn, so that both the white knight and the black bishop are attacked. Black wants to wreck White's pawn centre: e5 loses its support, and once bishop and knight are traded White's queenside pawns are scattered. White gets a half-open a-file and the initiative in return, so it is riskier than the main moves.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.Bd2.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square, since the e5 pawn covers f6, and keeps the bishop on b4 where it presses on c3. With the bishop on d2 ready to recapture on c3 without doubling pawns, Black has no reason to hurry the exchange.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.a3 B.strategy: Attacks the bishop on a5 and the c5 pawn together and so breaks the pin by force. White accepts sharp play, since the d4 pawn may have to be given up for time and pressure; Black's reply needs preparation.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.a3 B.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Retreat Variation, Armenian Line
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.a3 B.background: Named after its use by the Armenian grandmasters Rafael Vaganian and Smbat Lputian, although it had been used quite often before; it became popular in the 1950s and was deployed most notably in the world championship match between Smyslov and Botvinnik.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.a3 B.strategy: Counterattacks by taking on d4, which leaves both the bishop on a5 and the knight on c3 attacked. Black has grabbed a pawn and removed White's centre; White hopes to use the attack on the bishop and the open lines to take the initiative.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.a3 B.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Advance Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.a3 B.strategy: Recaptures towards the centre. White's doubled pawns strengthen the pawn centre and give a half-open b-file, and the bishop pair gives attacking chances against a kingside without its dark-squared bishop, but the long-term features of the structure favour Black.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.a3 B.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Advance Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.a3 B.strategy: The main move: develops the knight to a flexible square and keeps Black's castling options open. Against a queen attack on g7 Black plays for the centre and White's king; in quieter lines Black castles long and closes the queenside, to open the kingside where White's king stands.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.a3 B.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Classical Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.a3 B.strategy: Adds pressure on the e5 pawn and keeps the choice of knight development open. It often returns to the main line, but Black can use the extra flexibility to meet a queen sortie with a pawn move on the kingside instead of the usual knight move.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.a3 B.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Portisch-Hook Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.a3 B.strategy: Attacks the loose pawn on c3 at once and so forces White to respond before the kingside attack can start. It is the sharpest way to use the doubled pawns as a target, at the price of delaying Black's own development.

Develops the queenside knight and adds to the pressure on d4. It is playable and seen now and then, but it leaves the kingside knight at home, so Black is less flexible than in the main line when White sends the queen towards g7.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.a3 c.strategy: Takes the bishop that Black left en prise. After ...dxc3 the bishop and knight are traded, White's d4 pawn is gone and the black pawn on c3 stands deep in White's position, where it is a target. The a-file is half-open for White's rook.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.a3 c.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Maróczy-Wallis Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.a3 c.strategy: Takes the knight at once, so the piece White won with 6.axb4 is paid back. The pawn on c3 attacks b2, and once White takes it material is level. Black has swapped its dark-squared bishop for a knight and plays for activity against a loosened queenside and a king still in the centre.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.Bd2.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Bogoljubow Variation, Icelandic Defence
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.Bd2.strategy: Reinforces the e5 pawn and grabs kingside space, a bid for a broad pawn centre. It costs a tempo and does nothing about the pressure on d4 and c3: ...cxd4 at once attacks the knight, which the bishop on b4 is already bearing down on.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 Ne7 5.a3.strategy: Puts the question to the bishop at once. If it takes on c3, White gets the bishop pair and a broad pawn centre for doubled pawns, with the weakened g7 pawn as a target for the queen; if it retreats, it loses its pressure on c3.

Gives up the dark-squared bishop for the knight and doubles White's pawns before the bishop is driven back. The price is the dark squares on the kingside, which White's pieces will aim at; in return Black gets a closed position whose pawn structure favours it in the long run.

The only recapture, and a thematic one: White accepts doubled c-pawns for a strong pawn centre, a half-open b-file and the bishop pair. The structure gives Black targets on the queenside, while White's play comes on the kingside, where the dark squares are weak.

Hits the base of the pawn chain at once, the thematic follow-up now that the dark-squared bishop has gone. Black aims at d4 and c3 and can later close the queenside with ...c4, leaving the fight on the kingside, where White is trying to attack. The doubled pawns are Black's long-term trump.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.exd5 exd5 5..strategy: Develops the bishop on its natural diagonal, where it bears on h7 and prepares castling. White keeps the symmetrical structure; the usual way to unbalance it is a3, provoking the exchange on c3 and leaving an asymmetrical pawn structure after bxc3.

Develops the knight to a square from which it guards d5 and can reach f5 to block the bishop's diagonal or g6 to challenge a queen on h5. The cost is that h7 is guarded only by the rook, which invites a queen sortie, so Black must be alert on that diagonal.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.exd5 exd5 5..name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Exchange Variation, Canal Attack
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.exd5 exd5 5..strategy: Brings the queen out so that it and the bishop on d3 both bear on h7, which only the rook guards, and Black has to meet the threat at once. But the queen is exposed early and can be driven off with gain of time, so the attack achieves little against accurate defence.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Ne2 dxe4 5.a.strategy: Asks the bishop to decide at once, and the answer shapes the whole line. If Black takes on c3, the knight recaptures and White plays on for development and the bishop pair; if the bishop retreats, White simply wins the pawn back.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Ne2 dxe4 5.a.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Alekhine Gambit Accepted
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Ne2 dxe4 5.a.strategy: Takes the knight and keeps the extra pawn. Black gives up the dark-squared bishop and hands White the bishop pair and a lead in development, which is all the compensation White has; whether it is enough is the question of the whole line.

Retreats and gives the pawn back: White recaptures on e4 at once, so Black avoids the gambit's dangers and keeps both bishops. The game is level, with a sound, undoubled structure for Black and a slight lead in development for White.

Regains the pawn at once, putting a knight on a strong central square. Material is level and White is a little ahead in development, so the gambit has bought time at no cost, though Black's position is sound and safe.

Develops with a threat: the knight attacks the one on e4, which no piece defends, so White has to deal with it at once. Black gets a normal French set-up, with the bishop on e7 ready for castling and a comfortable game.

Recaptures with the knight from e2, which is the point of 4.Ne2: White keeps its pawn structure intact. In return for the pawn it has the bishop pair and a lead in development, and it is Black who must now defend.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Ne2 dxe4 5.a.name: French Defence: Winawer Variation, Alekhine Gambit, Kan Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Ne2 dxe4 5.a.strategy: Keeps the extra pawn and hits d4, which is attacked twice and defended once. Black develops with a threat, but is still a pawn up with an unfinished kingside and has to find a way to complete development against White's bishops and open lines.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Ne2 Nf6 5.Bg.name: French Defence: McCutcheon Variation, Wolf Gambit
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Ne2 Nf6 5.Bg.strategy: Pins the knight on f6 to the queen and threatens to push e5, offering the e4 pawn for speed. Black can take it: after ...dxe4 the knight on c3 is pinned against the king and cannot retake, so White must prove that the lead in development pays.
